title: Fellowships and Freedom
subtitle: and Air Mattresses
html:
Two weeks after our last installment, I was sleeping on a thinly veiled matrix of torture devices (springs) in Harvard’s student housing. I’d just been accepted into the Cambridge Boston Alignment Initiative’s (CBAI) AIxBiosecurity Research Fellowship (rolls off the tongue, I know), so I moved across the country with only what I could bring on a plane—two suitcases and a guitar. For the first time since getting accepted into graduate school in the spring of 2024, I felt like I had some agency. The amorphous blob of worldly-things-that-I-could-affect finally moved when I poked it. Few things deplete one’s will to act like a steady stream of evidence that no action they take will affect the world. At last, the stream was interrupted.

The CBAI fellowship marked my pivot away from medtech (because trying to get a job in medtech left me jobless for a year) and toward biosecurity. For context, biosecurity is roughly defined as the field of protecting against biological risks. At the time of writing this, I’m working with SecureBio, a two-pronged non-profit working on “securing the future against catastrophic pandemics.” Under SecureBio’s mentorship, I’ve been developing better tools to understand AI biocapabilities.

In my short time with SecureBio, a gaggle of things are making themselves painfully clear:

  1. Trading time for money is a losing game.

  2. Starting my own business feels inevitable.

  3. You don’t need someone’s permission.

  4. Looking cringe is necessary for growth.

I’m acting on these realizations—seeking mentorship, wearing Crocs and sandals and wife-beaters, and doing things my way; not because my way is “better”, but because it is mine. It’s taken me an embarrassingly long time to learn that no one is living my life but me, so it is okay to live it how others would not. Stranger still, many people don’t learn this lesson until they’re old and wrinkly. This is why old people are so fun: they have no shame. Nothing illuminates the silliness of self-consciousness like death.

Now, I’m living in South Boston (a.k.a. Southie) after living in Harvard Square for 4 weeks, followed by Kendall Square for 4 more weeks. Nothing from my apartment in Wisconsin has arrived yet, so I’m 5 weeks into sleeping on an air mattress, eating on my floor, and taking meetings with my laptop propped up on an unopened monitor box because my desk is in moving company purgatory. While this may sound unpleasant from the outside, I’m enjoying it. It’s quieting—there are fewer distractions, and it gives me a funny story to tell. It also highlights how few things we need to be content. An air mattress, a Pyrex bowl, a spoon, and a guitar can go a long way.

That’s all for now, though.

More to come.

Cheers,

Charlie
